newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine traders say grain export ban creeps back.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine traders say grain export ban creeps back.

text.p: Ukrainian grain traders said on Wednesday the country was continuing to prevent grain exports despite earlier statements to the contrary.
Officials ordered an investigation into the allegations.
Traders accused the government of quietly ordering state-owned elevators to lock up grain so that it could fill its purchase contracts in a poor harvest year.

"The government keeps saying there is no problem with exports and that there legally can be no ban on exports," Yuri Federenko, head of the Ukrainian Agrarian Mercantile Exchange (UAME) brokers' association, told angry traders at the weekly trading session.
Activity on Ukraine's exchanges ground to a halt in early August over what traders said was a ban on grain exports, but resumed earlier this month.
Now the problem has resurfaced, traders said.
Only one transaction took place on Wednesday at the UAME, Ukraine's largest exchange.
"It's not over yet," said Bohdan Chomiak, a representative of the Washington-based Chemonics research group.
President Leonid Kuchma ordered Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko to report on the situation by September 27.
The government in August denied issuing official orders halting exports, but said such instructions might have been issued informally in some provinces.
The government has said it requires five million tonnes for domestic needs and that it hopes to export three million tonnes.
The official net grain harvest forecast this year stands at a poor 28 million tonnes.
Kuchma's order, circulated at the UAME session, was accompanied by a letter from a top Economy Ministry official outlining traders' grievances.
It acknowledged that grain exports were stopped, paralysing the UAME and cutting its August trade volumes to a quarter of last year's levels.
Traders said Kuchma's order to Lazarenko would leave the government plenty of time to fill its own contracts.
"On September 27, you can say that the ban has been officially lifted," Chomiak said.
He said the government had at least acknowledged the situation, even though it has denied that it is responsible.
Brokers unable to fulfil forward contracts were liable for breach of contract without written government evidence of force majeure.
Only about eight percent of grain is bought and sold on the relatively new exchange system, while the rest is bartered.
